source.preview:
# Chapter I: Down the Rabbit-Hole

Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice “without pictures or conversation?”

So she was…

# Chapter I: Down the Rabbit-Hole

Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice “without pictures or conversation?”

So she was…

tiles.title: Alice
tiles.claim: Alice is reached through her thoughts: she complains, wonders and boasts to herself, and acts before she reasons about it.

evidence.text: never once considering how in the world she was to get out again
thought Alice to herself

tiles.friction: Eight paragraphs make a thin cast. The Rabbit’s “hides” reads what the chapter withholds rather than anything shown, and Alice’s “wants” leans on a single complaint in ¶2.
tiles.energy: Idle until something odd crosses her path, then all motion.
tiles.wants: Something worth her attention: pictures, conversation, a rabbit with a watch.
tiles.hides: Little; she says what she thinks, aloud or to herself.

tiles.title: White Rabbit
tiles.claim: The Rabbit is all surface and schedule: it speaks once, checks its watch and vanishes, and its strangeness only registers with Alice afterwards.

evidence.text: TOOK A WATCH OUT OF ITS WAISTCOAT-POCKET
it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this

tiles.friction: Eight paragraphs make a thin cast. The Rabbit’s “hides” reads what the chapter withholds rather than anything shown, and Alice’s “wants” leans on a single complaint in ¶2.
tiles.energy: Pure hurry, seen only from outside.
tiles.hides: Where it is going and why; the chapter does not say.

tiles.title: her sister
tiles.claim: The sister is reading a book without pictures, and the chapter leaves her on the bank the moment the Rabbit runs by.

evidence.text: she had peeped into the book her sister was reading

tiles.friction: Eight paragraphs make a thin cast. The Rabbit’s “hides” reads what the chapter withholds rather than anything shown, and Alice’s “wants” leans on a single complaint in ¶2.
tiles.energy: Present only as a book Alice cannot share.

tiles.title: Narrative voice
tiles.claim: The narration stays with Alice but talks over her shoulder: parenthetical asides comment on what she says, and capitals do the shouting.

evidence.text: (Which was very likely true.)
There was nothing so VERY remarkable in that

tiles.friction: The asides make the narrator a presence of its own, so “close on Alice” may undersell it; and eight paragraphs leave the voice little room to change.

traits.label: Point of view
traits.value: Third person, close on Alice, with a narrator who steps aside to comment.

traits.label: Distance
traits.value: Close, yet the narrator keeps an amused distance in its asides.

traits.label: Register
traits.value: Conversational and wry, with capitals for emphasis.

traits.label: Sentence music
traits.value: Long sentences that run on through clauses, broken by short exclamations.

said.text: Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!

said.text: and what is the use of a book

tiles.title: Victorian children’s fantasy
tiles.claim: A child, a talking animal and a hole into somewhere else, told by a narrator who winks at the reader over the child’s head.

evidence.text: Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!
(Which was very likely true.)

tiles.friction: Genre pulls toward a destination and a reason for the fall, and these paragraphs keep both out of view. “Victorian children’s fantasy” also leans on the book’s reputation, which eight paragraphs alone do not prove.

tiles.title: Literary nonsense
tiles.claim: Logic bends without alarm: the fall is slow enough to read the shelves, and a falling girl worries about a jar of marmalade.

evidence.text: she did not like to drop the jar for fear of killing somebody

tiles.friction: Genre pulls toward a destination and a reason for the fall, and these paragraphs keep both out of view. “Victorian children’s fantasy” also leans on the book’s reputation, which eight paragraphs alone do not prove.

tiles.title: Portal fantasy
tiles.claim: A threshold under a hedge leads somewhere else, though in these paragraphs nothing has been reached yet.

evidence.text: a large rabbit-hole under the hedge

tiles.friction: Genre pulls toward a destination and a reason for the fall, and these paragraphs keep both out of view. “Victorian children’s fantasy” also leans on the book’s reputation, which eight paragraphs alone do not prove.

tiles.title: Survival thriller
tiles.claim: The situation has the furniture of peril, a fall with no way back, but nothing in the telling is afraid.

evidence.text: never once considering how in the world she was to get out again

tiles.friction: Genre pulls toward a destination and a reason for the fall, and these paragraphs keep both out of view. “Victorian children’s fantasy” also leans on the book’s reputation, which eight paragraphs alone do not prove.
tiles.nearMiss: A fall with no way out matches; the dread a thriller promises is absent, and the fall is a pleasure.

tiles.title: Reader promise
tiles.claim: Something strange will be followed, and wonder will win out over fear.

evidence.text: burning with curiosity

tiles.friction: Genre pulls toward a destination and a reason for the fall, and these paragraphs keep both out of view. “Victorian children’s fantasy” also leans on the book’s reputation, which eight paragraphs alone do not prove.

tiles.title: The white hart
tiles.claim: The Rabbit plays the white beast that draws a follower across a threshold, though nothing in these paragraphs is a quest.

evidence.text: a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her
she ran across the field after it

tiles.friction: Any fall invites the underworld, so the descent may be the reading’s reflex more than the chapter’s; and the white hart rests on one white animal in ¶3.

stances.note: A white animal crosses the path and is followed out of the ordinary world.
She follows from curiosity, not as a hunter, and nothing is to be caught.

tiles.title: The descent to the underworld
tiles.claim: The oldest shape of a journey below is taken up and emptied of dread: the underworld begins as a well lined with cupboards.

evidence.text: falling down a very deep well
she had plenty of time as she went down to look about her

tiles.friction: Any fall invites the underworld, so the descent may be the reading’s reflex more than the chapter’s; and the white hart rests on one white animal in ¶3.

stances.note: A fall below the ground, into somewhere else.
The way down is slow and furnished: she reads the shelves as she falls.

tiles.title: The empty jar
tiles.claim: The jar she takes from the shelf is labelled as one thing and holds nothing. What else down the well might be named one thing and hold another?

evidence.text: it was labelled “ORANGE MARMALADE”, but to her great disappointment it was empty

tiles.friction: Later chapters may say who the Rabbit is late for, so that door may already be shut; and “Nobody at home” leans on one exclamation in ¶8.

tiles.title: Late for what?
tiles.claim: The Rabbit is late, and the chapter never says for what. Who is waiting at the other end of the hole?

evidence.text: I shall be late!

tiles.friction: Later chapters may say who the Rabbit is late for, so that door may already be shut; and “Nobody at home” leans on one exclamation in ¶8.

tiles.title: Nobody at home
tiles.claim: Alice pictures how brave they will think her at home. Who is at home, and does anyone there know she has gone?

evidence.text: How brave they’ll all think me at home!

tiles.friction: Later chapters may say who the Rabbit is late for, so that door may already be shut; and “Nobody at home” leans on one exclamation in ¶8.

frictions.friction: Genre pulls toward a destination and a reason for the fall, and these paragraphs keep both out of view. “Victorian children’s fantasy” also leans on the book’s reputation, which eight paragraphs alone do not prove.
Any fall invites the underworld, so the descent may be the reading’s reflex more than the chapter’s; and the white hart rests on one white animal in ¶3.

setAside.title: Persephone
setAside.reason: No one takes her below: she jumps in after the Rabbit herself.

setAside.title: Orpheus
setAside.reason: Nobody has been lost below, so there is no one to bring back.

frictions.friction: Later chapters may say who the Rabbit is late for, so that door may already be shut; and “Nobody at home” leans on one exclamation in ¶8.

tiles.friction: Later chapters may say who the Rabbit is late for, so that door may already be shut; and “Nobody at home” leans on one exclamation in ¶8.

frictions.friction: Genre pulls toward a destination and a reason for the fall, and these paragraphs keep both out of view. “Victorian children’s fantasy” also leans on the book’s reputation, which eight paragraphs alone do not prove.
Any fall invites the underworld, so the descent may be the reading’s reflex more than the chapter’s; and the white hart rests on one white animal in ¶3.

setAside.title: Persephone
setAside.reason: No one takes her below: she jumps in after the Rabbit herself.

setAside.title: Orpheus
setAside.reason: Nobody has been lost below, so there is no one to bring back.
